product.title: Egyptian Arabic 101 - A1 (English Edition)
product.description: Twenty Assimil-style self-study units that take you from zero in Egyptian Arabic (العامية المصرية) — the Arabic dialect most widely understood across the Arab world, thanks to Egyptian films, songs, and TV series. Written exactly the way Egyptians write, with a full pronunciation guide under every line of dialogue, word-for-word translations that show how Egyptian builds its sentences, grammar notes, vocabulary, exercises, and an answer key. Includes a pronunciation guide, an A1 grammar summary, the forty most common verbs, and a page on how Egyptian differs from Fusha. Perfect for learners who can read the Arabic script but have never used it to speak — and for complete beginners too: each unit targets the point that trips learners up most, from ج pronounced as g to question words placed at the end of the sentence.

blocks.text: If you can already read the Arabic script — from Qur'an classes, school, or a family background — you hold an advantage almost no learner of Egyptian Arabic outside the Arab world has: before opening this book, your eyes already recognize ب، ت، ث and can sound out اَلْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ without thinking. That head start cuts weeks off your journey, and this book is designed to use it from page one. If you're starting from zero, the pronunciation guide under every line will carry you.

But there's one fact we should be honest about on page one as well: the Arabic of the Qur'an, books, and the news — Fusha — is not the language Egyptians use to order coffee, haggle with a taxi driver, or joke with the neighbors. Step off the plane in Cairo and say مَاذَا تُرِيدُ؟ with perfect i'raab, and people will understand you — and know at once that you learned from a book. What they say themselves is عايز إيه؟

That isn't broken Arabic. It's living Arabic. Every Arabic speaker grows up with two layers: Fusha for what is written and read aloud, 'ammiyya for what is spoken. Both are legitimate, both are used every day, and no native speaker thinks one is more correct than the other. This book teaches the second layer.

And among all the Arabic dialects, Egyptian holds a special place: it's the one understood from Morocco to Oman without translation. The reason is simple — nearly a century of Egyptian films, songs, and TV series has reached every home in the Arab world. Kuwaitis know Umm Kulthum's songs; Moroccans watch Egyptian Ramadan dramas. Learning Egyptian is buying one ticket that works in twenty-two countries.

blocks.title: Good news for beginners
items: **No i'raab at all.** All the case endings ـُ ـَ ـِ and the tanween that make grammar classes painful are gone. كِتَابٌ جَدِيدٌ becomes كتاب جديد, read *kitaab gidiid*, full stop.
**No word for "is".** أنا طالب = "I student", and that's a complete sentence. English needs "am"; Egyptian simply doesn't.
**No verb "to have".** Possession works with a little word, عند. So عندي كتاب = "at-me a book" — "I have a book". Once you see the trick, it's easier than it looks.
**Possession has its own word: بتاع.** الكتاب بتاعي = "the book of mine". Egyptians use it much like English uses "of mine" — far easier than the Fusha idafa.

**You already know some of the words.** Egyptian has borrowed freely from European languages, and many of them will look familiar: أوتوبيس، بنك، تليفون، دكتور، بلكونة — bus, bank, telephone, doctor, balcony.

blocks.text: There are surprises too, and it's better you know now than in unit seven. First: the letter ج is pronounced as a hard **g** in Egypt, not "j". جميل is not *jamiil* but *gamiil*. Second: the letter ق almost always turns into a catch in the throat — قهوة is not *qahwah* but *’ahwa*. Third: question words go at the **end** of the sentence. "What's your name?" is not مَا اسْمُكَ but اسمك إيه؟ — literally "your name what?"

Those three sound like obstacles, but they're actually the door. Once your ear accepts that ج is g and ق is a catch, half the Egyptian songs and films that used to sound foreign suddenly become easy to follow. This book puts all three in unit one instead of saving them for later.

One more decision you should know about: the Egyptian text in this book is written **without vowel marks**, exactly the way Egyptians write on WhatsApp, on shop signs, and in film subtitles. In exchange, every line of dialogue and every word in the vocabulary lists comes with a full pronunciation guide. The reason is practical: you'll never meet vowel marks in the real world, and depending on them leaves you stranded the moment you leave the book. The pronunciation guide here is a walking stick you can slowly throw away.

Twenty units, each built around one complete dialogue, and each aimed at the point that trips learners up most. Do one unit in twenty to thirty minutes, reread the dialogue aloud the next day, then move on. Yalla bina — let's get started.

This book follows the Assimil method: instead of memorizing a word list and then using it, you go straight into one complete conversation and take it apart from the inside. The order in which you work matters.
One unit, one sitting

items: Read the dialogue once from top to bottom without stopping. Don't worry if a lot is still unclear — it isn't time yet.
Reread it while following the pronunciation line. Say it out loud. A mouth that moves remembers far better than an eye that reads.
Only now read the notes and the grammar boxes. At this point you already have real sentences to hang the rules on.
Skim the vocabulary list quickly — it's there for reference, not to be memorized in one sitting.
Do the exercises with the dialogue page covered. The answer key is at the end of each unit; check it after you finish, not halfway through.
The next day, before starting a new unit, reread yesterday's dialogue out loud. Five minutes. This is the part people skip most often, and it's the part that matters most.

blocks.text: Signs used in this book

Each line of dialogue has four layers: the Egyptian text, the pronunciation, a natural translation, and a **literal** translation in small letters. That last one is not correct English and isn't meant to be — it shows how Egyptian builds its sentences, word by word.

blocks.title: If you've already studied Fusha
items: Don't throw anything away. Ninety percent of the vocabulary is the same, and the verb patterns belong to the same family. What changes is pronunciation, word order, and about thirty of the most frequent words, which have their own Egyptian forms.
But keep your hands off the i'raab endings. Saying أنا طالبٌ in a Cairo coffee shop sounds like ordering a burger in the language of a courtroom.
The "Egyptian and Fusha" page that follows sums up all the differences in one table. If you come from a Fusha background, start there.

front.title: Pronunciation: the signs used in this book

blocks.text: The pronunciation is written in ordinary Latin letters, not phonetic symbols. Long vowels are written double (*aa, ii, uu*), and the four "heavy" (emphatic) consonants get a dot underneath — *ṣ, ḍ, ṭ, ẓ* — so they're never confused with *sh*, *th* or *dh*. Beyond that, you only need to watch two quote marks and the letters that change their sound in Egypt.

blocks.text: The letter ق is still pronounced **q** in some words that come from Fusha and feel formal — القرآن *al-Qur’aan*, or القاهرة *al-Qaahira* on the news. This book writes words exactly as people actually say them, so you'll see both.

blocks.text: The difference is real: ع is made by tightening the throat while voicing, whereas ء just cuts the sound off for an instant. Egyptians will still understand you if you swap them — but these are two letters that tell words apart, so it pays to get used to them from the start.
The other letters

Long vowels are written double: *aa, ii, uu* (*aa* as in *father*, *ii* as in *see*, *uu* as in *food*). Egyptian also has two long vowels that Fusha doesn't, born from the old *ai* and *au* — written *ē* and *ō*: بيت *bēt* (house — *ē* as in *they*), يوم *yōm* (day — *ō* as in *go*). If you're used to saying *bait* and *yaum*, this is one of the quickest changes that will make you sound Egyptian. Short *e* is as in *bed*, short *o* as in *for*.

blocks.title: Word stress
items: Egyptian stresses the syllable that **contains a long vowel**, or the **second-to-last** syllable if there's no long vowel: *ma-DRA-sa*, *ki-TAAB*, *’ah-WA*.
Stress isn't marked in this book, to keep the pronunciation clean. The rule above covers almost every word, and the rest will stick through listening.

front.title: Egyptian and Fusha: ten differences you'll notice

blocks.text: This page is for those who've already touched Fusha. If you're starting from zero, skip it and come back later — everything is taught step by step inside the units.

blocks.text: Notice the pattern running through the whole table: Egyptian swaps endings for **small stand-alone words**. Possession no longer works through changing endings but through بتاع. Tense no longer works through the inner pattern of the word but through بـ and حـ. Negation no longer uses five different words but one wrapper, مـ...ش.

For English speakers, that direction of change happens to be very convenient: English also works with small stand-alone words — "of", "will", "not", "-ing". In many ways, Egyptian Arabic builds its sentences more like English than Fusha does.

blocks.title: Thirty words that are completely different
items: Most Egyptian and Fusha vocabulary is the same. The words that differ are precisely the most frequent ones — and once these thirty are in, you can follow a simple conversation.
**Time:** دلوقتي *dilwa’ti* (now) · النهاردة *innaharda* (today) · إمبارح *imbaari7* → *imbaarih* (yesterday) · بكرة *bukra* (tomorrow) · لسه *lissa* (still, not yet).

**Sentence fillers:** حاجة *haaga* (something, thing) · كده *kida* (like that) · أوي *’awi* (very) · بس *bas* (but; enough) · شوية *shuwayya* (a little) · كتير *kitiir* (a lot) · عشان *‘ashaan* (because; so that).

**What you'll hear every five minutes:** خلاص *khalaaṣ* (done, that's it) · معلش *ma‘lesh* (never mind; sorry) · يلا *yalla* (come on) · طيب *ṭayyib* (okay then) · ماشي *maashi* (OK) · إن شاء الله *insha’allah*.
That last one isn't small talk. In Egypt إن شاء الله goes with almost every promise, and leaving it out sounds arrogant.

blocks.text: These pages sum up everything used in the twenty units. Use them for review, not for learning something for the first time.
Pronouns and possessive endings
The word بتاع — stand-alone possession

The word بتاع agrees with the thing owned, not the owner: masculine بتاع *bitaa‘*, feminine بتاعة *bitaa‘it*, plural بتوع *bituu‘*. All the endings in the table above can attach to it — الكتاب بتاعي، العربية بتاعتها، الفلوس بتوعنا.
Present-tense verbs, with and without بـ

The form without بـ doesn't stand on its own. It's used after عايز، لازم، ممكن، بحب، ينفع — and only there. This is the number-one mistake foreign learners make: عايز **بشرب** is wrong; the correct form is عايز **أشرب**.
Past-tense verbs
Negation
Question words — always at the end
Demonstratives and prepositions
Demonstratives always come **after** the thing they point to, and that thing must carry الـ, as in الكتاب ده، الشنطة دي، الولاد دول.

If you only have time to memorize one table from these pages, take the بـ and حـ table. It's what separates a correct sentence from one that's only almost correct, and it's in every sentence you'll say today.
Forms given: the past tense for هو (the dictionary form in Egyptian), then the present tense for هو with بـ. From these two forms you can work out every table on the previous pages yourself.

If you've reached this page after working through twenty units, you now have something most people who study Arabic for years don't: the ability to open your mouth. You can greet, order, haggle, ask the way, talk about yesterday and make promises about tomorrow. That's A1, and it's a real stepping stone.

What matters most now isn't the next book but your ears. Egyptian is a lucky language: material is plentiful and free. Start with things where people speak slowly and the pictures help — family TV series, cooking channels, travel vlogs from Cairo — not the news, which is in Fusha.

blocks.title: Three habits that lift A1 to A2
items: **Twenty minutes of watching every day with Arabic subtitles on.** Not English subtitles. Your eyes will start linking sounds you already know with unvowelled writing, and that's the next big leap.
**Write three sentences about your day, every day, in Egyptian.** Mistakes are fine. What matters is that your mouth and your hand move in the same language.
**Find one person to talk to once a week.** Egyptian has almost no graded reading material — it's a spoken language. One hour of talking beats ten hours of reading.

blocks.text: There's also a road that runs backwards, and it's typical of the Arab world: once your 'ammiyya is solid, Fusha becomes much lighter. You already have the vocabulary and a feel for the verb patterns; all that's left is the endings and the style. Many people find Egyptian first, Fusha later a more human path than the other way around.

Don't carry that weight — متشيلش هم *matshilsh hamm*. Learning a language isn't a race, and Egyptians are among the most generous speakers there are toward foreigners who try. Say a word or two, and see for yourself how doors open. بالتوفيق.
